records.name_note: Sources split in structure but converge on "lead plant" as the species-distinguishing lead, and "False indigo" is excluded as a lead. NC State's Common Name(s) field lists four entries alphabetically (False indigo, Lead Plant, Leadplant Amorpha, Prairie Shoestring), and its first entry also matches the first name in the page's own title line, "Amorpha canescens (False indigo, Lead Plant, Leadplant Amorpha, Prairie Shoestring)"; NC State's own body prose calls the species "the lead plant" throughout and explains the name from the leaves' lead-dusted appearance. MoBot's displayed "Common Name:" field affirmatively designates "lead plant" as primary, with a Common Names tooltip behind it listing lead plant, leadwort, North American wild tea, downy indigobush. RHS's H1 is the bare binomial "Amorpha canescens" with "lead plant" as the plant-profile subtitle (also in the page title), and "leadwort, North American wild tea" under its separate Other common names heading. "False indigo," though it appears in NC State's list, is a genus-umbrella name -- MoBot states the genus Amorpha itself is "often called false indigo" for its resemblance to Indigofera -- not a species-distinguishing name; this catalog already uses the qualified forms "White False Indigo" and "Blue False Indigo" for Baptisia, so the bare umbrella name should not be presented as this species' lead.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: none of the three admissible sources with content for this species (NC State, MoBot, RHS) carry any toxicity information for Amorpha canescens — NC State's Plant Type Tags for this page (Ground Cover, Perennial, Shrub, Wildflower, Woody Plant) do not include 'Poisonous', so there is no NC State Poison block to capture, and RHS's page states no toxicity information.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max, day/night temperature fields, chill_damage_f, and cool_rest_note left null: this is an outdoor hardy shrub (NC State USDA zones 2a-9b; RHS Hardiness H7) and none of the admissible sources state foot-candle light levels, humidity percentages, air-temperature ranges, or a chill-damage onset temperature for it — RHS's H7 hardiness rating is a survival/zone rating, not a damage-onset figure, so per the schema rules it cannot be used for chill_damage_f.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source discusses fertilizing this species.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, and water_dormant_days_est left null: this is an in-ground native shrub and no admissible source frames its watering in day-interval or dry-down terms.

water_regime left null: MoBot's only structured moisture field is 'Water: Dry to medium', a mid-scale rating that per the schema rules cannot support keep_moist; its Culture prose ('Grow in average, dry to medium moisture, well-drained soil') and NC State's parallel prose ('sandy or rocky, well-drained soil') are cultivation/soil descriptions rather than watering instructions, so no clean water_regime enum value is supported.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max both left null: NC State's Soil pH field gives a closed 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' band, but RHS's pH field lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as all acceptable, so per the schema rule the closed band's ceiling and floor are both overridden and left open.

'False indigo' and 'Prairie Shoestring' and 'Leadplant Amorpha' all appear only in NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list (with 'False indigo' additionally being the umbrella name MoBot assigns to the whole genus Amorpha, and already used in this catalog for Baptisia) or in NC State's auto-generated one-alias-per-name pages (e.g. /plants/amorpha-canescens/common-name/prairie-shoestring), which carry no primacy of their own; none of them is treated as a lead name.

Only three of the ten admissible domains (plants.ces.ncsu.edu, plantfinder.mobot.org/missouribotanicalgarden.org, and rhs.org.uk) returned any content for Amorpha canescens; hgic.clemson.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, and fieldreport.caes.uga.edu had no dedicated or incidental coverage of this species found via search.

NC State's Common Name(s) field stacks five entries in alphabetical order (Allegheny Onion, Lady's Leek, Nodding Onion, Nodding Wild Onion, Wild Onion), and the browser page title repeats those same five names in the same order; its on-page heading is just the binomial. RHS gives only 'lady's leek' -- it appears as the subtitle beneath the Allium cernuum heading and again after the binomial in the page title; no 'onion' common name appears anywhere on the RHS page. MoBot's Common Name field and NC State's body prose converge on 'Nodding Onion', so that name is used here, with the RHS and MoBot-internal splits noted.

RHS's page does carry a 'Potentially harmful' badge reading "TOXIC to pets - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers," but per the task's scoping rule this is a wholly unscoped 'toxic to pets' mention that names no specific animal (no cat, dog, or other species named anywhere on the RHS page), so it cannot support toxic_to_pets=true. records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) list is a two-entry list ("Smooth Aster", "Smooth Blue Aster") whose order matches the page title parenthetical and the body prose, which opens "Smooth aster is a herbaceous perennial..." -- a valid lead. Missouri Botanical Garden's Common Name field reads "smooth aster", its body prose ("commonly called smooth aster") leads with the same name, and its Common Names tooltip renders the same two names, "smooth aster" and "smooth blue aster". records.name_note: Sources split on which name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) list for Liatris aspera carries a single entry, "Rough Blazing-star," matching both the page title parenthetical and the body prose, so it is a genuine lead rather than an alphabetization artifact. RHS's plant-profile subtitle likewise names it "rough blazing star," with a secondary "Other common names" field adding "tall gay feather" (not presented as primary). MoBot's affirmative "Common Name:" field, by contrast, displays "blazing star" alone -- a genus-umbrella name, since the sibling species already in this catalog, Liatris spicata, also carries "Blazing Star" as one of its own NC State common names, so it does not distinguish this species. MoBot's longer Common Names tooltip/popup behind that field (five stacked entries: blazing star, gay feather, gayfeather, rough blazing star, rough gayfeather) does include "rough blazing star" but marks no entry as primary. Given the genus-umbrella exclusion rule, "Rough Blazing Star" (led by NC State's and RHS's dedicated single-species pages) is used as the catalog common name rather than MoBot's umbrella "blazing star." No admissible source's structured field or page title used "Tall Blazing Star" or "Button Blazing Star" as a primary name for this species; those variants appeared only in non-admissible search-result aggregations and were not used.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail left null: none of the fetched admissible-source pages for Liatris aspera (NC State, MoBot, RHS) carry a poison/toxicity block, a Poisonous Plant Type tag, or a Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag for this species; NC State's Problems text for this species reads only 'No significant problems. Root rot can occur on to wet soils.'

soil_drainage left null: NC State's Soil Drainage tags for this species are 'Moist' and 'Occasionally Dry' -- not the bare Good-Drainage+Moist pair, and not a span across both occasionally-dry and occasionally-wet, so they don't meet either the fast or moderate trigger under the strict rule. RHS's Soil Moisture field says only 'Well-drained' (a bare, ambiguous statement per the rule) without the 'sharp/very/excellent' language required for 'fast', and MoBot's habitat description ('dryish soils') and structured Water field ('Dry to medium') are a tolerance trait, not a drainage statement. NC State also lists Clay as a tolerated soil texture, which the rule says rules 'fast' out. Left null rather than guessed.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists only an open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band with no Neutral/closed band to read a floor or ceiling from; RHS's pH field lists 'Neutral or Alkaline or Acid', confirming a wide tolerance and giving no numeric bound either.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a watering-statement or structured moisture field mapping cleanly onto the four-value enum. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Dry to medium', a mid/dry-leaning data point disclosed here rather than forced into an enum value.

direct_sun_hours_max, light_fc_min/good, humidity_need/pct, day/night temperature fields, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, and all fertilize_* fields left null: no admissible source for Liatris aspera specifically states these (only NC State's generic site-wide light-category legend gives hour ranges, which is excluded from use per the rules; hardiness-zone data from NC State (3a-8b), MoBot (Zone 3 to 8) and RHS (Hardiness H4) exist but are zone/survival ratings, not chill-damage onset temperatures or day/night temperature targets).

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes part_shade: NC State's own structured Light field additionally lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)' for this species, but MoBot's and RHS's structured sun fields list only Full sun, so part_shade was excluded per the rule that a value excluded by two of three sources' structured sun fields is left out.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, and water_dry_down_target left null: this is an in-ground perennial and no admissible source frames its watering in day-interval or check-depth terms.

"Tall Blazing Star" and "Button Blazing Star" (named in the task prompt as possible page splits) were not found as primary or structured-field names on any of the three fetched admissible pages (NC State, MoBot, RHS) for Liatris aspera; RHS's only secondary name is "tall gay feather". Clemson, Penn State, University of Maryland, UF/IFAS (EDIS and Ask IFAS), and UGA fieldreport searches returned no dedicated Liatris aspera content -- only genus-level or Liatris spicata material -- so those domains contributed no fields to this record.
